implementation_notes: Active Record implements STI out of the box: when the table has a column named type (configurable via inheritance_column), subclasses of the model are stored in the parent's table with the class name in that column, and Company.where(...).first returns a Firm or Client instance without any mapper code. The framework owns the mapping, so the classic mapper classes disappear and the model class carries both behaviour and its discriminator value. The trade-offs are framework-specific: the type attribute is written from the class name, the column is part of every record's attribute set, and STI only triggers when the column actually exists.
code_sketch:
class Company < ApplicationRecord; end
class Firm < Company; end
class Client < Company; end

Firm.create(name: "37signals")            # companies row with type = "Firm"
Company.where(name: "37signals").first     # => #<Firm ...>
pitfalls: New subclass records are dirty: because the type attribute is derived from the class name, Firm.new.changed? is true where Company.new.changed? is false - callbacks, validations and tests that assume a clean new record can break when STI is switched on.
The stored discriminator is the class name, so renaming or namespacing a subclass changes the meaning of every existing row; do it as a data migration, not as a code refactor.
Without a type column nothing happens: the subclasses behave as plain Ruby inheritance over the parent's table and every query returns the parent class, which silently defeats the design.
All subclasses share one table, so a column added for one subclass appears as a nullable attribute on every sibling model (and on the parent's rows).
